issues.legal_issue: A party who performs additional work under a contract without intending it to be gratuitous may receive compensation for its value when the other party obtains a benefit, even if the alleged oral agreement fixing payment is not proved.
material_facts: A building contractor performed additional construction work that was not covered by the written agreement.
The parties each alleged a different oral agreement governing payment for the additional work, and neither alleged agreement was accepted.
The additional work was not performed gratuitously, and the property owner obtained its benefit.
The contractor claimed payment for the additional work under the alleged oral agreement.
issues.conclusion: The contractor was entitled to compensation under section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, even though the alleged oral agreement was not proved; awarding compensation on that basis did not substantially depart from the claim made.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a person who lawfully does something for another, without intending to do so gratuitously, and the other person enjoys its benefit, is entitled to compensation or restoration of the thing done. Failure to prove an express agreement fixing payment does not prevent an award under section 70. The court relied on no earlier cases.

rule.if: contractor_extra_work_claim and work_outside_written_contract and not intended_as_gift and recipient_received_benefit

predicates.contractor_extra_work_claim: A contractor seeks payment for work performed for another person beyond the work covered by their written contract.
predicates.work_outside_written_contract: The work for which payment is sought was not covered by the written contract.
predicates.not_intended_as_gift: The person who performed the work did not intend to provide it gratuitously.
predicates.recipient_received_benefit: The recipient obtained and enjoyed a benefit from the work.

issues.definition: When a contractor seeks payment for work outside a written contract, did not intend to provide it as a gift, and the recipient obtained its benefit, the contractor is entitled to reasonable compensation.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court need not interfere with directions for assessing compensation for additional work when the assessment is based on rates supported by evidence and shown to be reasonable.
material_facts: The High Court directed that compensation for additional work be assessed using rates contained in a bill.
A witness for the owner acknowledged that those rates were current market rates for similar construction work.
The High Court considered the rates not excessive and directed an engineer to assess the amount payable.
issues.conclusion: The direction to assess compensation using those rates did not involve a serious error justifying appellate interference.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court may leave an assessment direction undisturbed where the selected rates are supported by testimony as current market rates for similar work and are not shown to be excessive. The court relied on no statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.appeal_challenges_assessment_direction: A party appeals a direction for assessing compensation for work performed.
predicates.rates_supported_as_current_market_rates: Evidence establishes that the rates selected for assessment reflect current market rates for similar work.
predicates.rates_not_shown_excessive: The selected rates are not shown to be excessive.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an assessment direction, the rates are supported as current market rates, and they are not shown to be excessive, the direction is not interfered with.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot pursue compensation for defective work as a set-off in related suits after its separate claim for that compensation has been dismissed and no appeal has been brought against the dismissal.
material_facts: The owner brought a separate suit seeking compensation for loss allegedly caused by defective work.
The High Court dismissed that suit, and the owner did not appeal the dismissal.
The owner then sought to raise the same compensation claim as an equitable set-off in the contractor's related suits.
The owner had not pleaded equitable set-off in the written statements in those suits.
issues.conclusion: The owner could not reagitate the compensation claim in the related suits.
issues.legal_principle: A party whose substantive claim has been dismissed and who has not appealed that dismissal cannot seek to reagitate the same claim in companion suits; in this case, no equitable set-off had been pleaded in those suits. The court relied on no statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

rule.if: related_claims_in_companion_suits and separate_compensation_claim_dismissed and not appeal_against_dismissal and not setoff_pleaded

predicates.related_claims_in_companion_suits: A party seeks to raise a compensation claim as a set-off in suits related to the dispute.
predicates.separate_compensation_claim_dismissed: The party previously brought a separate suit for the same compensation claim and that suit was dismissed.
predicates.not_appeal_against_dismissal: The party did not appeal the dismissal of the separate claim.
predicates.not_setoff_pleaded: The party did not plead the set-off in the related suits.

issues.definition: When a party raises a compensation claim as a set-off in related suits, its separate claim has been dismissed, it did not appeal, and it did not plead the set-off, the dismissed claim cannot be reagitated as a set-off.
